{"commits":[{"authoredDate":"2026-09-19T01:15:35Z","authors":[{"email":"jerimiah797@gmail.com","id":"MDQ6VXNlcjE1ODQyODI=","login":"jerimiah797","name":"Jerimiah Ham"}],"committedDate":"2026-09-19T01:15:35Z","messageBody":"Xcode 27 ships a guest HID daemon, `dtuhidd`, and its Device Hub attaches
it to every booted simulator. The guest answers by disconnecting the
legacy touch, button and keyboard services quern drives, and never
reconnects them: it re-adds an already-invalidated service reference,
records it as connected, and never retries. Everything else keeps
working -- reads, screenshots, open_url, app launches -- so the device
looks healthy while nothing anyone does reaches it.

Keyboard is lost whenever the daemon has attached. Touch and buttons
depend on whether the guest's input layer started before or after the
attachment, so typing can be dead while tapping still works, and a busy
machine loses more often.

The mechanism and the repair are tddworks/baguette#78's. facebook/idb's
"Detect a crashed dtuhidd instead of discarding HID events" documents a
second route to the same silence -- the daemon aborting during boot --
and puts the handover at CoreSimulator 1155.4. This machine is 1171.7.

What this does:

- `server/device/sim_input.py` reads the guest notify state and, when
  asked, clears it and restarts backboardd. That order is the repair:
  clearing alone reconnects nothing, and clearing *after* the restart
  hands the new backboardd the edge that causes the disconnect.
- A boot quern performs waits for Device Hub to attach, then repairs,
  while nothing is running. The wait is what makes it work: repairing
  the moment boot returned was undone by an attachment that had not
  happened yet -- measured, the state went back to 1 and typing was
  dead. With no Device Hub running there is nothing to wait for, so
  that boot pays nothing.
- `POST /api/v1/device/ui/restore-input` and the matching
  `restore_simulator_input` tool do it on request, for a simulator that
  was already booted. Not automatic there: it restarts SpringBoard and
  kills the user's apps.
- Taps, swipes, typing and button presses warn once per device when the
  state says the services were taken. A warning rather than a refusal,
  because the state is not conclusive: a simulator booted before Device
  Hub started kept working with the state set, so refusing on it would
  refuse input that works.

The real fix is to drive the DTUHID transport, as idb now does. This is
the stopgap.

Live, on an iPhone 16 Plus (iOS 18.6), Xcode 27.0:

- restore-input on a suppressed simulator: state 1 -> 0, and typing
  lands where it did not before.
- Boot through quern with Device Hub running: state 0 afterwards, and
  typing lands. Boot takes ~18s, including the wait and the repair.
- The repair holds with Device Hub running: state stayed 0 over 20s.

Six findings on #234, all of them right.

Three of the seven input paths never asked whether input could land.
`tap_element` -- the most-used of them, and the one whose sweep started
all of this -- resolved a device twice and wrote to it on both paths
without checking; `scroll_to_element` and `clear_text` likewise. All
seven check now, and a test walks the list by name so an eighth cannot
be forgotten quietly.

Two repairs of the same simulator could interleave. The sequence that
matters: both clear the state, one restarts backboardd and reports
success, the other fails and puts the state back to 1 during its
rollback, so the caller is told the services are back while the guest
says otherwise. `restore_legacy_input` now holds a per-udid lock across
the clear, the restart, the rollback and the wait. Per-udid rather than
global, so two simulators still repair in parallel.

A timed-out `notifyutil -s` was treated as though it had done nothing,
but the write may land before the kill -- leaving the state cleared over
disconnected services, which is the one combination nothing can detect.
`_spawn` reports a timeout distinctly now, and a timed-out clear puts
the state back.

The cache recorded a verdict nobody reached. A wait that expired with
Device Hub running stored "healthy", which stops every later probe; so
did an unreadable state. It now stores only a repair that worked or a
healthy simulator on a machine with no Device Hub running.

The endpoint answered 500 for an Android or physical device, because the
mapper turns an unmatched DeviceError into one. It is a 400: asking a
phone for a thing only simulators have is the caller's mistake.

main is merged, which also resolves the duplicate `### Fixed` heading.

A verdict outlives the device it described. `_input_checked[udid] = True`
from an earlier boot survived a reboot, and a boot whose probe then
failed or timed out left it in place -- so the first input call skipped
its check and a simulator whose services had been taken never warned.
Both the verdict and the cooldown are cleared before the boot probe.

`_spawn` caught TimeoutError but not CancelledError, so cancelling a
repair cancelled the wait and left the child running. The repair lock
was then released over a live `kickstart`, and the next repair could
overlap it -- which is the interleaving the lock exists to prevent, one
level down. Cancellation now kills and reaps the child before
re-raising.

The two tests that wait on those guards are bounded, per the path
instructions: without the guard they hung the suite, and a hang says
less than a failure.

Review of 5f6274a Code review plus a live check. I created and booted **my own** simulator (`quern-rev234-review`, iPhone 16 / iOS 18.6), probed it, ran the repair on it, then shut it down and deleted it. The iPhone 16 Plus and iPhone 17 Pro were not touched, nothing ran against `~/.quern` or port 9100, and nothing was pushed. Tests pass (23). I also probed the module and controller directly in a `git archive` copy. The mechanism, the repair and the boot-path ordering all check out live. **3 findings I'd fix before merge, 6 lower.** Since this is the only review, the first one is worth a second opinion: it's the case where the change makes a failure *quieter* than it was. ### Medium-high **F-1. A half-applied repair silently disables the detection it came with.** (Verified.) `server/device/sim_input.py`, `restore_legacy_input`: the clear lands, the kickstart fails, `DeviceError` is raised — and the notify state is now **0** with the services still disconnected. Every later read says "not suppressed", so `_warn_if_input_is_suppressed` records the device as healthy and no tap ever warns again. I drove exactly that: after the failed repair, the state read False and a subsequent tap cached `{"SIM": True}` with no warning. Failure scenario: the user shuts the simulator down (or it wedges) between the two `simctl spawn` calls — the case you asked about. Before the repair attempt they got a warning naming the problem and the fix; after it they get silence. That's the failure shape this PR exists to end. Suggestion: on a kickstart failure, best-effort re-set the state to 1 so the symptom stays visible, and/or record the failed repair per-udid so the warning keeps firing regardless of what the state says. **F-2. "Could not ask" is cached as "fine".** (Verified.) `server/device/controller_ui.py`, `_warn_if_input_is_suppressed`: `self._input_checked[resolved] = not suppressed`. With `suppressed is None` that stores `True`, and `.get(resolved) is not None` then skips the check for the life of the process. One transient failure — a spawn timeout, or the first tap landing while the device is still coming up — permanently disables detection for that device. In a probe, a first answer of None left the probe awaited once and the cache set, and a genuinely suppressed state afterwards was never seen. `legacy_input_is_suppressed` goes out of its way to distinguish asked-and-answered from could-not-ask; this drops that distinction at the one place that consumes it. Cache only a real bool. **F-3. The other documented route to the same silence is invisible, and costs 22s per boot.** (Verified.) The module's own docstring cites idb's crashed-`dtuhidd` case, where the daemon aborts during boot and HID events are discarded with the state never going to 1. On that path: - `wait_for_device_hub_to_attach` polls for its full 20s — measured **22.3s added to the boot**, 9 polls — and returns False; - no repair runs, the device is recorded as healthy, and later taps never warn. So the boot pays the whole wait precisely when input is broken, and says nothing. Same arithmetic for any runtime that doesn't publish the key: I confirmed `notifyutil -g ` exits 0 printing ` 0`, so it reads as a confident False. Worth either shortening the wait, or treating "Device Hub is up but never attached" as its own suspicious state rather than a clean bill of health. ### Low **F-4. `_spawn` discards stderr, so failures are reported with a guessed cause.** (Verified live.) Against a shut-down simulator, `simctl spawn` exits 149 and prints `Process spawn via launchd failed because device is not booted` — on stderr, which `_spawn` captures and drops. The caller gets "Could not clear com.apple.coredevice.dtuhidd.active on 92C571A8; simulator input cannot be restored **while Device Hub holds it**", naming a cause nothing checked. Capture stderr into the error, and consider refusing early when the device isn't booted. **F-5. Nothing serialises the repair.** (Verified.) Two concurrent calls interleave as clear, clear, kickstart, kickstart — two SpringBoard restarts. A boot-path repair racing the endpoint does the same. A per-udid lock would make it idempotent. **F-6. `_input_checked` survives a shutdown.** `shutdown()` doesn't drop the entry, so a simulator rebooted outside quern keeps its old verdict. Acceptable as you say — the boot path repopulates it — but it's one line in `shutdown()` and removes a stale-state class entirely. **F-7. The docstring's None claim doesn't match the tool.** (Verified live.) `legacy_input_is_suppressed` says an older simulator that never heard of the key "answers the same way as one that is not booted". It doesn't: an unknown key returns rc 0 and ` 0`, so that case answers **False**. The behaviour is defensible; the comment isn't. **F-8. The agent still sees `{"status": "ok"}`.** The warning goes to the server log, which an MCP client never reads. #231's conclusion was "input that cannot land must not report ok", and the CHANGELOG says taps "warn once per device … rather than reporting a success that never happened" — but the response the caller receives is unchanged. Since the state isn't conclusive, refusing would be wrong; carrying `input_suppressed: true` plus the restore hint in the tap/swipe/type responses would let an agent act on it. At minimum, soften the CHANGELOG sentence. **F-9.
